vignette:
Margaret sits in the chair across from me, her hands folded neatly in her lap, the way an auditor might hold a report she's about to deliver. She is seventy-five, married for fifty-two years to Thomas, a retired engineer. She still works part-time as an auditor for a small regional firm, though she tells me she's thinking of retiring. "I can't focus like I used to," she says, her voice steady but thin. Her PCL-5 score is 74, a number that matches the weight I see behind her eyes.

She begins her story not with the war, but with the smell of mangoes. "On the first day of the bombing," she says, "I was standing at a market stall near the harbor. The air was thick with dust and the sweetness of ripe mangoes. That smell never left me." She was thirty-four then, a young auditor working for a government agency in a small coastal town in the Pacific. Her country had just become entangled in a regional conflict she didn't fully understand. "The sirens came at noon. I remember dropping my clipboard. Everyone started running. I ran too, but I didn't know where."

She found shelter under a concrete stairwell in a nearby government building. For three hours she crouched there, knees to chest, as mortar shells pounded the streets. A woman beside her was praying in a language Margaret didn't recognize. The woman had a small child pressed against her chest. "I still see the child's face," Margaret whispers. "He was so quiet. Just stared at me with huge brown eyes. Later, I learned that whole block was destroyed. I never saw them again."

The bombing ended after six weeks, but the war continued for another year. Margaret returned to her job, but something had shifted. She became meticulous to the point of rigidity-triple-checking every column, every decimal. Her supervisors praised her for it. "I thought if I could just control the numbers, I could control everything else," she tells me. "But I couldn't. At night, I'd lie awake and smell mangoes." She started having dreams where she was back under that stairwell, the child's eyes watching her, the woman's prayers becoming a scream.

Now, four decades later, she lives in a quiet suburb in Australia. She and Thomas emigrated fifteen years ago. She thought the distance would help. It didn't. "Every time I hear a helicopter," she says, "I freeze. My heart pounds. I have to sit down. Thomas knows. He turns up the television." She avoids the fruit section at the supermarket. Mangoes make her nauseous. Crowded places-shopping malls, church, even the local library-send her into a cold sweat. She has stopped attending her weekly book club. She tells people she's "just getting older." But inside, she feels like she's still thirty-four, still trapped under that stairwell.

At work, she struggles. She can no longer maintain the relentless focus that once defined her. Numbers blur. She forgets basic formulas. Last month, she made a significant error on a client's tax return-her first in forty years. "I had to redo it three times. My manager asked if I was okay. I said I was tired." She dreads the end of the month, when deadlines loom. Her hands tremble when she holds a calculator. She has started leaving early, telling herself she's doing half-days. But she knows it's because she can't bear the fluorescent lights, the silence of the office, the way the flickering bulb reminds her of the emergency strobes from that day.

Her mornings are the hardest. She wakes at 4 a.m., drenched in sweat, the sound of an explosion still ringing in her ears. She lies still, trying to breathe, telling herself she is safe. Thomas sleeps beside her, unaware. She has never told him the full story. "He knows I was in a war," she says. "But he doesn't know about the mangoes, or the child's eyes. I don't want him to see me like that. I'm supposed to be the one who holds everything together." She pauses, and for the first time, her voice cracks. "But I'm not holding anything together anymore."

She does not say she is broken, but I see it in the way she flinches when the chair creaks, in the way she checks her watch every few minutes, as if expecting the next explosion at any moment. Margaret is still an auditor, still a wife, still a woman who survived. But survival, for her, has become a kind of prison-one where the past is always a second away from crashing into the present.
